newsitem.title: USA: Former Mexican official denies taking drug bribes.
newsitem.headline: Former Mexican official denies taking drug bribes.

text.p: A former Mexican deputy attorney general on Friday denied allegations he took bribes for protecting drug-traffickers smuggling tons of cocaine and marijuana into the United States.

But Mario Ruiz Massieu admitted for the first time that he owned a black Ford Grand Marquis, similar to the one in which a former police bodyguard earlier testified he had placed two suitcases full of drug money.

The testimony came in the fifth day of a civil trial in which the U.S. government is attempting to confiscate a $9 million Texas bank account belonging to Ruiz Massieu. Prosecutors alleged the money came from drug traffickers.
An eight-person jury was to begin deliberations in the case on Saturday.

In closing arguments on Friday evening, defence attorney Tony Canales accused prosecutors of "arrogance" for having frozen Ruiz Massieu's money two years ago and said, "This case reeks of government overreaching."
He urged the jury to "take on the government" by finding that Ruiz Massieu should keep the $9 million.
Prosecutor Jesse Rodriguez said: "This case is about 'show me the money, show me what the legitimate source of the money is.' They can't do it."
In often defensive and combative testimony, Ruiz Massieu vehemently denied any contact with Mexican drug lords.
"Never," Ruiz Massieu said when asked if he had taken bribes from drug traffickers. "Absolutely never."

In key testimony earlier this week, former police bodyguard Raul Macias said in August 1994 he placed two suitcases full of cash in a dark blue Ford Grand Marquis outside the Attorney General's headquarters in Mexico City.
Inside the car, he testified, was Ruiz Massieu. The money came from a 10-ton shipment of cocaine seized by police in the northern state of Zacatecas, then sold back to traffickers.

Ruiz Massieu testifed on Thursday he did not own a dark blue Grand Marquis, but on Friday, when shown a document by prosecutor Jesse Rodriguez, admitted he owned a black one. Rodriguez asked if it were possible the colours were similar enough to be confused.
"It was blue, not black. The colour blue is different from black, at least in Mexico," Ruiz Massieu said.
Ruiz Massieu also denied allegations he tipped off drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego hours before federal agents raided his ranch hideout in northern Mexico in 1993.
"I don't know Juan Garcia Abrego. I would never have given him a tip," Ruiz Massieu told the eight-person jury.
Ruiz Massieu backed away from earlier testimony in which he implied he had nothing to do with drug enforcement, which would have ruled out his providing protection for traffickers.

He admitted he had investigated drug cases, but said fighting drugs was not his primary responsibility. At one point, he blurted out: "The most important drug-traffickers arrested in Mexico, I arrested."

Ruiz Massieu said the money sought by the government was brought to the United States for safekeeping and included part of the family's fortune and lavish government bonuses paid to him and his brother Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, general secretary of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI.

Ruiz Massieu said he fled Mexico because of threats following publication of his book charging the PRI with obstructing his investigation into the September 1994 assassination of brother Jose Francisco.
"I believe that the PRI was putting up obstacles to the investigation," said Ruiz Massieu, who resigned his post as deputy attorney general and a member of the PRI in late 1994.

Mexican authorities said Mario Ruiz Massieu covered up the fact that his brother's murder was ordered by Raul Salinas de Gortari, the jailed brother of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and fled Mexico to escape charges.
"With total frankness, absolutely false, that's another lie," he said of the coverup allegation.
Ruiz Massieu lives in New Jersey under house arrest while he awaits an upcoming deportation hearing.
